lesson_title: England in the fourteenth century: society, church and trade
content_html:
England on the Eve of War

In 1337, England was a deeply ordered society. Most people never travelled more than a few miles from their birthplace, and their lives were shaped by three interlocking institutions: the manor, the parish church, and the serf system that kept most people tied to the land. Understanding this world is essential because the crises of plague and revolt that followed make little sense without it.

The Manorial System

English rural life was organised around the manorial system. At its head stood the lord of the manor, who owned the land and administered justice through the manorial court. Beneath him were free tenants who paid rent in money, and below them the villeins — unfree peasants who owed their lord a set number of days’ work each week on the lord’s “demesne” land. In return they were given strips of land to farm for themselves.

Serfdom was the defining reality of most people’s lives. A serf could not leave the manor, marry without the lord’s permission, or pass on their land freely. They were legally his property. Historians estimate that roughly half of England’s rural population in the early fourteenth century were villeins or serfs bound to manors in this way.

Key Fact

A villein (serf) could not leave the manor, marry, or pass on land without the lord’s permission. They owed labour — typically two to three days per week on the lord’s demesne — as well as rents in grain or money.

The Role of the Church

No institution touched everyday life as deeply as the parish church. The parish was the centre of the community — it recorded births, marriages and deaths, provided charity, and gave the agricultural year its rhythm through the great festivals: Christmas, Easter, Midsummer and Harvest. In a largely illiterate society, the priest was one of the few educated men most people would ever meet.

The Church was also enormously wealthy. By the fourteenth century the Church owned roughly a third of all land in England. Monasteries, cathedrals and parish churches collected tithes — a tenth of each parishioner’s produce — as well as fees for baptisms, marriages and burials. This wealth made the Church a powerful landlord as well as a spiritual authority.

Faith shaped how people understood suffering, illness and death. Disease was widely seen as God’s punishment for sin, and the only remedies available were prayer, pilgrimage and the sacraments of the Church. This worldview would become dangerously important when the Black Death arrived in 1348.

The Church commanded unquestioned authority at every level of society. The Pope in Rome claimed spiritual supremacy over all Christian kingdoms, and English bishops sat in the House of Lords alongside the great nobles. The Archbishop of Canterbury was among the most powerful men in the kingdom.

Yet the Church faced growing criticism. Some priests were poorly educated or corrupt, collecting tithes without providing adequate spiritual care. Wealthy monasteries attracted accusations of greed. These tensions would deepen over the fourteenth century — John Wyclif’s later challenges to Church authority did not come from nowhere but built on long-standing popular resentment.

The Wool Trade

England’s greatest source of wealth in the fourteenth century was wool. English wool trade supplied the looms of Flanders (modern-day Belgium and the Netherlands), where it was woven into fine cloth and sold across Europe. By the 1330s, England exported around 30,000 sacks of wool per year, generating enormous customs revenue for the Crown.

The wool trade shaped politics as well as economics. Edward III desperately needed the revenue from wool customs to fund his wars in France. He also needed the goodwill of Flemish merchants and cloth-workers — which partly explains why the Flemish towns’ preference for English wool made them potential allies against France. The relationship between trade and war was close and constant throughout this period.

Key Fact

Wool was England’s most valuable export. Customs duties on wool provided a significant share of royal income, and the Flemish cloth industry’s dependence on English wool gave Edward III diplomatic leverage when seeking allies against France.

The Position of Women

Women in fourteenth-century England occupied a legally inferior position. Under common law, married women had no separate legal identity — they could not own property, make contracts, or bring lawsuits in their own name. A wife’s legal person was absorbed into her husband’s.

In practice, life was more complex. Peasant women worked alongside men in the fields, as well as spinning, brewing, baking and managing the household. Widows could hold land and run businesses in their own right. Women in towns sometimes worked in trades and crafts, sometimes as independent traders known as “femmes soles.” Noble women could manage vast estates in their husbands’ absence. Yet access to education, the Church hierarchy and political power remained entirely closed to women at every level of society.

The gap between rich and poor in fourteenth-century England was enormous. A great baron might command thousands of acres and dozens of dependent manors; a villein family scratched a living from a few strips of land subject to weather, disease and the lord’s arbitrary demands. The nobility and gentry ate varied diets rich in meat and imported spices; peasants depended on bread, pottage and ale, with meat a rare luxury.

Yet the system was not entirely static. Some free peasants accumulated land and became prosperous yeomen. Skilled tradesmen in towns could rise to modest comfort. The wool trade created a new merchant class whose wealth rivalled that of minor nobles — and who would become increasingly influential in Parliament. It was this social complexity — people with grievances, aspirations and some leverage — that would make the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 possible.

lesson_title: Causes of the Hundred Years' War
content_html:
Why Did England and France Go to War?

The Hundred Years’ War — the series of conflicts fought between England and France from 1337 to 1453 — did not begin from a single cause. It grew from decades of competing dynastic claims, disputed territories and diplomatic rivalries. Understanding why war broke out in 1337 requires looking at the interlinked pressures on both Edward III and the French Crown.

Edward III’s Claim to the French Throne

The most dramatic grievance was Edward III’s personal claim to the French throne. When the French king Charles IV died in 1328 without a male heir, Edward — as the son of Isabella of France and the grandson of Philip IV of France — argued he had the strongest dynastic claim to be the next king of France.

The French nobility rejected this argument. They invoked an ancient legal custom, the Salic law, which excluded inheritance through the female line. Instead, they crowned Philip of Valois as Philip VI. Edward initially accepted this — he paid homage to Philip for his French lands — but as relations deteriorated, he pressed his claim as a pretext for war.

Key Fact

Edward III claimed the French throne through his mother Isabella, daughter of Philip IV of France. When Charles IV died heirless in 1328, the French nobles rejected Edward’s claim and crowned Philip VI instead, planting a dynastic grievance that Edward later used to justify war.

The English Lands in France: Aquitaine

At the root of the conflict was the long-standing problem of English-held land in France. Since 1154, English kings had held territories in France, and by the fourteenth century Aquitaine in south-west France was the most important. It was extraordinarily profitable — the wine trade alone generated significant customs revenue — and English kings were determined to keep it.

But holding Aquitaine meant English kings were also feudal vassals of the French Crown for those lands — an awkward position when relations broke down. Philip VI repeatedly sought to undermine English control of Aquitaine, supporting local French lords who disputed English authority. In 1337, Philip formally confiscated Aquitaine, claiming Edward had failed in his feudal obligations. This act made war almost inevitable.

Aquitaine was not just a symbol of royal prestige — it was an economic asset. The region’s vineyards supplied a thriving wine trade with England, and the port of Bordeaux was one of the busiest in northern Europe. English merchants, traders and the Crown itself derived significant income from this commerce. Losing Aquitaine would have been a major financial as well as political blow to Edward III and his war-making capacity.

The Auld Alliance: France and Scotland

England’s strategic position was complicated by the Auld Alliance between France and Scotland. This alliance, which stretched back to 1295, meant that when England threatened France, Scotland would threaten England’s northern border — and vice versa. Edward III had already fought a war in Scotland in the 1330s to impose his preferred candidate, Edward Balliol, on the Scottish throne.

The Franco-Scottish alliance was therefore a genuine strategic threat. If Edward committed his forces to France, the Scots — backed by French support — could raid northern England. This forced Edward to maintain a military presence in the north even while fighting in France, stretching his resources considerably.

Key Fact

The Auld Alliance meant France and Scotland were mutual allies against England. While Edward III fought in France, Scotland — backed by French diplomacy and resources — could threaten England’s northern border, forcing Edward to fight on two fronts simultaneously.

Philip VI’s Role and the Confiscation of 1337

Philip VI was not a passive figure waiting to be attacked. He actively sought to weaken English power in France. He supported David II of Scotland against Edward’s preferred candidate, encouraged French lords in Aquitaine to resist English rule, and in May 1337 formally confiscated Aquitaine from Edward, declaring him a rebellious vassal.

This confiscation was the immediate trigger for the war. Edward III responded by formally declaring himself king of France in 1337 and launching a military campaign. The war that followed would last, with interruptions, until 1453 — long after Edward III himself was dead. But the causes laid down in the years before 1337 — dynastic rivalry, disputed territory, Scottish entanglement and French provocation — shaped every aspect of the conflict that followed.

Edward III’s aims were not simply to press his claim to the French throne — that may have been as much a propaganda device as a genuine ambition. His more immediate objectives were to secure Aquitaine against French encroachment, to end French support for Scotland, and to demonstrate his military prowess to the English nobility, who expected a king to lead his armies. War also offered the prospect of plunder, ransom and glory — incentives that mattered to the military class who would have to fight it.

lesson_title: The course of the war: Crécy, Calais and Poitiers
content_html:
England’s Military Advantage

In the first two decades of the Hundred Years’ War, English armies achieved a series of astonishing victories against a larger and wealthier enemy. These victories were not accidents. They reflected specific tactical choices — above all the use of the longbow — and a deliberate strategy of devastating the French countryside to undermine French royal authority and force battle on English terms.

The Chevauchée: Burning France into Submission

The primary English offensive strategy was the chevauchée. English armies would ride through French territory burning villages, destroying crops, looting towns and killing livestock. The aim was not simply plunder — it was political. The French king was expected to protect his subjects. If he could not, his authority and prestige would suffer, potentially encouraging rival French lords or the common people to question his rule.

Chevauchées also had practical military benefits. They forced the French to respond, either accepting the humiliation of doing nothing or risking battle on ground chosen by the English. English commanders understood that their opponents’ heavy cavalry — French knights on horseback — were at a severe disadvantage when forced to charge uphill against massed archers in a prepared defensive position.

Key Fact

The chevauchée was both an economic weapon and a propaganda tool. By burning the French countryside, English armies demonstrated that Philip VI (and later John II) could not protect their subjects — striking at the king’s authority as well as his treasury.

The Battle of Crécy, 1346

The Battle of Crécy, fought on 26 August 1346, was the defining demonstration of English tactical superiority. Edward III positioned his army on a ridge near the village of Crécy in northern France, with his longbowmen on the flanks. When the French cavalry charged, the English archers unleashed a devastating storm of arrows. The French charged approximately fifteen or sixteen times but were repulsed each time with terrible losses.

The longbow proved decisive. Welsh and English archers could fire up to twelve arrows per minute, creating a density of fire that French armour could not withstand at close range. The French also deployed Genoese crossbowmen as allies, but their weapons were slower and less effective, and they were cut down or abandoned when the battle turned against France. Philip VI himself fled the field. The victory was complete.

The English longbow was typically made from a single stave of yew, around six feet long. It required years of training to use effectively — medieval skeletons of archers show distinctive bone deformations caused by drawing the bow repeatedly from boyhood. Its range of over 200 yards and rate of fire of up to twelve arrows per minute made it incomparably more effective in massed use than crossbows or the shorter bows used elsewhere in Europe. English law required free men to practise archery regularly, ensuring a large pool of trained archers available for military service.

The Siege of Calais, 1346–1347

Following Crécy, Edward III besieged the port of Calais. The town held out for almost a year before surrendering in August 1347. Its capture was strategically vital: Calais provided England with a permanent military and commercial bridgehead on the French coast, making future campaigns far easier to supply and reinforce. Edward expelled the French population and resettled the town with English merchants and craftsmen.

The story of the six burghers of Calais — leading citizens who offered themselves to Edward to spare the town — became one of the most famous episodes of the war. According to contemporary accounts, Queen Philippa interceded with Edward to spare their lives, and he relented. England held Calais until 1558.

Key Fact

Calais, captured in 1347 after a year-long siege, gave England a permanent base on the French coast. It was a supply depot, a military staging post, and a commercial centre. England held it for over two hundred years, until 1558.

The Battle of Poitiers, 1356, and the Black Prince

Ten years after Crécy, England won an even more dramatic victory at Poitiers. Edward, the Black Prince, led a chevauchée deep into France in 1356. Caught by a much larger French army under King John II near Poitiers, he chose a strong defensive position. On 19 September 1356, the French cavalry charged uphill against English and Welsh archers and were again devastated.

More dramatically, King John II of France was captured on the battlefield — one of the most valuable prisoners of the medieval era. His ransom was set at three million gold crowns, a sum so enormous that it strained French royal finances for years. The victory at Poitiers, combined with Crécy, demonstrated that English tactics were consistently superior to French heavy cavalry in pitched battle.

The capture of King John II at Poitiers gave Edward III enormous leverage. In 1360, the Treaty of Brétigny was agreed. France ceded full sovereignty over Aquitaine (expanding it significantly beyond its previous extent) and agreed to pay a ransom of three million gold crowns for John II. In return, Edward renounced his formal claim to the French throne — though this proved temporary, and the claim was revived when the treaty terms were not fully honoured. Brétigny marked the high point of English success in the first phase of the war.

lesson_title: The arrival and immediate impact of the Black Death
content_html:
The Deadliest Catastrophe of the Middle Ages

In the summer of 1348, a disease arrived in England that would kill, by most historians’ estimates, between a third and a half of the entire population within two years. The Black Death was not a single disease but at least two distinct and deadly forms of plague, and nothing in medieval experience had prepared people for an epidemic on this scale.

How the Black Death Arrived in England

The Black Death originated in Central Asia and spread westward along trade routes in the 1340s. It devastated the Byzantine Empire and the Mediterranean world before reaching Sicily in late 1347. By the summer of 1348 it had crossed France and arrived in England, probably through the ports of the south coast — Melcombe Regis (now part of Weymouth) in Dorset is often cited in contemporary sources as one of the first places affected, probably in June 1348.

The disease spread rapidly along trade and communication routes. By 1349 it had reached the north of England and Scotland. The speed of spread reflected England’s well-developed internal trade networks, the movement of merchants, pilgrims and soldiers, and the presence of rats and fleas in virtually every settlement.

Key Fact

The Black Death reached England through southern ports in the summer of 1348 and spread across the whole country within approximately eighteen months. Historians estimate that between one third and one half of England’s population died, though precise figures are uncertain and vary by region.

The Strains of Plague: Bubonic and Pneumonic

The Black Death was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. The most common form was bubonic plague, spread by fleas feeding on infected rats and then biting humans. Its key symptom was the “bubo” — a painful swelling at the lymph nodes in the armpit, groin or neck. Without treatment, approximately half to two thirds of those infected died within days.

Equally feared was pneumonic plague, which attacked the lungs and spread through the air when infected people coughed. Pneumonic plague was almost universally fatal and spread even faster than bubonic, requiring no flea or rat as intermediary. The combination of the two forms meant the epidemic had virtually no natural brake.

Several factors made England particularly vulnerable. Population density in towns meant fleas and rats were ubiquitous. Poor sanitation — waste often disposed of in streets or rivers — created ideal conditions for disease. Trade routes and pilgrim roads moved infected individuals across the country quickly. Monasteries and hospitals, the main centres of care for the sick, concentrated infected people in one place, inadvertently accelerating transmission. Malnutrition, common among poorer peasants, weakened resistance. Finally, people had no understanding of how the disease actually spread, so they took no effective preventive action.

Contemporary Views on the Cause

In the absence of any understanding of bacteria or infection, fourteenth-century people interpreted the Black Death through the frameworks available to them. The most widespread medical explanation was the miasma theory, which held that disease was caused by bad or poisoned air rising from rotting matter, swamps and corrupted water. Physicians recommended burning aromatic herbs and avoiding low-lying ground to escape the miasma.

Religious explanations were equally powerful. Across Europe, many clergy and laypeople interpreted the plague as God’s punishment for human sin. This led to intense penitential activity: fasting, confession, pilgrimage, and prayer. Some people sought to appease God through self-flagellation — groups of flagellants travelled across Europe whipping themselves publicly to show their contrition.

Key Fact

Most fourteenth-century people believed the Black Death was caused either by poisonous air (miasma theory) or by God’s punishment for sin. Neither explanation led to effective preventive action — and some responses (mass gatherings for prayer, flagellant processions, pilgrimages) may have actively spread the disease further.

Scapegoating and Violence Against Jewish Communities

In parts of mainland Europe, the search for explanations led to violent persecution. Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells and causing the plague. Pogroms — organised violent attacks — swept through hundreds of Jewish communities in the Holy Roman Empire and France from 1348 onwards, killing thousands of people. In England, Jewish communities had been expelled entirely in 1290 under Edward I, so this particular wave of persecution did not occur there. Nevertheless, the pattern of scapegoating minorities in times of catastrophe was a significant feature of the European response to the Black Death.

The immediate human impact was overwhelming. Whole villages were abandoned. Priests refused to administer the last rites for fear of infection; some clergy fled their parishes. Entire families died within days. Contemporary chroniclers described the horror of seeing neighbours, relatives and colleagues dead in the streets. The Church, which was meant to provide comfort and spiritual care, found itself overwhelmed: so many priests died that the Church struggled to replace them and had to lower its usual educational requirements for ordination.

lesson_title: Legacy of the Black Death: labour, wages and the Statute of Labourers
content_html:
Death Rebalanced the Economy

When approximately one third to one half of England’s population died in 1348–1349, the survivors found themselves in a world transformed. Land that had been cultivated for centuries stood empty. Villages shrank or disappeared entirely. And for the first time in living memory, those who worked the land had leverage — because there were simply not enough people to go around. The labour shortage that followed the Black Death was one of the most economically significant consequences of the epidemic.

Why Survivors Had Power: Wages and Mobility

Before the Black Death, England’s population had been growing for over a century, and the surplus of agricultural labour had kept wages low and lords in a strong position. Peasants competed for scarce land and would accept poor conditions rather than go without. After the epidemic, this relationship was reversed.

Lords desperate to find workers to harvest their crops and tend their estates had to offer better terms. Wages for agricultural labourers rose sharply. Some surviving serfs — bound legally to their lords’ manors — simply left, knowing they could find work elsewhere and that lords were too short of hands to pursue them rigorously. Rents fell as lords competed to attract tenants for their empty land. The rent decline was significant in some areas, reducing the income of the landowning class.

Key Fact

After the Black Death, the massive reduction in population created a labour shortage that shifted economic power towards surviving workers. Wages rose, rents fell, and many serfs found they could leave their manors without being effectively stopped — a fundamental change from conditions before 1348.

The Statute of Labourers, 1351

The ruling class responded rapidly to these changes. In 1351 Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers. Its aims were clear: wages were to be fixed at the levels that had prevailed before the Black Death, labourers were forbidden to leave their place of work to seek higher pay elsewhere, and employers who paid more than the legal rate could be fined.

The Statute of Labourers was an attempt by the ruling class — landowners, nobles and the Crown — to reverse the economic gains that survivors had made and restore the pre-plague labour market. It made explicit what serfdom had always implied: that the state would use legal force to keep workers in their place and wages at the level lords preferred.

The Statute of Labourers was enforced with varying success across England. Local Justices of the Peace were charged with applying it, and some prosecutions were brought against both workers demanding higher wages and employers who paid them. However, in practice it proved extremely difficult to enforce in all areas. Lords who needed workers badly enough quietly paid over the limit, knowing that a fine was better than no harvest. Workers who moved on took advantage of a labour market that was working in their favour. The Statute was resented deeply, and its aggressive enforcement in the late 1370s and 1380s became one of the specific grievances that fuelled the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381.

Effects on Survivors: Art, Culture and Medicine

The Black Death left a profound mark on culture as well as economics. Art and literature became saturated with images of death. The memento mori tradition — artwork and poetry that reminded viewers of the inevitability of death — flourished. The “Danse Macabre” (Dance of Death) appeared across Europe as a visual motif in which skeletons danced with people of every rank, from pope to peasant, showing that death was the great leveller. In England, this tradition influenced poetry, church paintings and sculpture throughout the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

Medicine changed more slowly. Since miasma theory persisted as the dominant explanation for disease, physicians continued to recommend the same remedies — herbal treatments, bloodletting, and avoidance of bad air. However, some practitioners did notice that people who came into close contact with the sick were more likely to fall ill, an empirical observation that pointed towards contagion theory even if it was not yet clearly formulated. The scale of the epidemic also created pressure to establish more hospitals and training facilities for physicians in some European countries, though the pace of genuine medical progress was slow.

Key Fact

The Statute of Labourers (1351) attempted to fix wages at pre-Black Death levels and prevent workers from moving. Because it explicitly tried to reverse the economic gains survivors had made, it created deep and lasting resentment among the peasantry — a direct cause of the anger that drove the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381.

Serf Mobility and the Decline of the Old Order

Despite the Statute, the long-term trend was against the lords. Serf mobility increased across the second half of the fourteenth century, even if the law still defined such movement as illegal. Lords increasingly accepted the practical reality that holding onto serfs by force was too costly when workers were needed. By the end of the fourteenth century, many lords were converting labour obligations into money rents — a shift that gradually eroded the economic foundations of serfdom even before it was formally abolished.

England’s population did not recover to its pre-Black Death levels until well into the sixteenth century. In the short term, this meant fewer mouths to feed but also fewer hands to work — some marginal land went out of cultivation and was converted to sheep pasture, which required much less labour. The wool trade benefited as a result. In the longer term, the sustained labour shortage shifted the balance of economic power across English society, eroding the old certainties of serfdom and contributing to the gradual emergence of a more mobile wage-labour economy.

lesson_title: Peasant discontent: long and short-term causes
content_html:
Why 1381? Building Towards Revolt

The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 did not erupt from nowhere. It was the product of decades of accumulated grievances stretching back to the Black Death and even earlier — combined with a specific set of short-term triggers in the late 1370s and early 1380s. Understanding both the long-term causes (the structural injustices of medieval English society) and the short-term catalysts (the Poll Tax, the French Wars) is essential for analysing why this particular moment produced revolt.

Long-Term Causes: The Issue of Serfdom

At the core of the revolt was the continued existence of serfdom. As explored in the previous lesson, the Black Death had created a labour shortage that gave surviving peasants real economic leverage. Many expected that the practical decline of serfdom would be formalised — that they would be freed from their legal obligations to their lords. Instead, the Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to restore the pre-plague order and keep wages down.

Over the following three decades, the tension between peasants who felt they had earned their freedom through their indispensable labour and lords who used the courts to enforce serfdom built steadily. Manorial court records from the 1360s and 1370s show increasing numbers of cases where lords prosecuted peasants for leaving their manors or refusing to perform labour obligations. This legal pressure was a constant source of resentment.

Key Fact

The long-term causes of the Peasants’ Revolt included the continued enforcement of serfdom after the Black Death, the Statute of Labourers (1351) attempting to reverse wage gains, and decades of resentment at the gap between peasants’ economic reality and their legal status as unfree servants of their lords.

The Religious Ideas of John Ball

One of the most influential voices of peasant discontent was John Ball. Ball was a wandering priest who had been repeatedly imprisoned for preaching without licence. His message was simple and explosive: God made all people equal; serfdom was therefore not divinely ordained but a human invention imposed by the rich to exploit the poor.

Ball’s most famous expression of this idea was his rhyme: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?” — arguing that at the beginning of the world there were no lords and no serfs, only working people. This egalitarian message resonated deeply with peasants who had seen their practical importance to the economy grow while their legal status remained that of property. Ball was in prison at the time of the revolt but was broken out by the rebels, becoming one of its leading voices.

Ball’s ideas intersected with a broader religious ferment in late fourteenth-century England. The theologian John Wyclif (c. 1328–1384) was developing critiques of the Church’s wealth and authority that would later inspire the Lollards. While Wyclif himself was a university theologian and not directly connected to the revolt, the wider climate of questioning Church authority — especially the wealth and worldliness of senior clergy — fed into the atmosphere of discontent that produced 1381.

The Cost of the French Wars

By the late 1370s, the Hundred Years’ War had turned dramatically against England. The gains of the Treaty of Brétigny (1360) had been steadily eroded by French counter-attacks under Charles V. English armies were being driven out of territory won in the previous generation, and the cost of military campaigns was enormous. The Crown needed money, and it needed it fast.

The ordinary taxation of the period fell heavily on the poorest. Parliamentary subsidies, which funded the wars, were assessed on moveable goods — meaning peasants who owned some property paid, while the very poorest contributed nothing and the very richest paid proportionally less than their wealth warranted. The wars drained resources from communities already struggling, and the lack of decisive military victory made the taxation feel like exploitation without return.

Key Fact

The failing French Wars of the late 1370s created a fiscal crisis. Parliament imposed three Poll Taxes between 1377 and 1381 to fund military campaigns. The third Poll Tax of 1380 — collected in 1381 — was set at one shilling per head for every person over fifteen, regardless of wealth, and its deeply unfair flat rate was the immediate trigger for revolt.

The Poll Taxes of 1377-1381

Three Poll Taxes were levied between 1377 and 1381 to fund the French Wars. The first two were less resented because they were graduated — the wealthy paid more. The third Poll Tax, passed in 1380 and collected in early 1381, was deeply different: it imposed a flat rate of one shilling on every person over fifteen. For a lord, one shilling was trivial; for a peasant family, it could represent a week’s wages. Many communities simply refused to pay or hid people from tax collectors.

When the government sent out commissioners to investigate evasion and collect the unpaid tax in 1381, the result was explosive. In Essex and Kent — areas where the Statute of Labourers had been especially aggressively enforced — the arrival of tax commissioners became the final spark.

The Role of Wat Tyler

Wat Tyler emerged as the leading figure of the Kentish rebels in 1381. His exact background is uncertain, but he proved an effective military organiser, leading the march on London and negotiating with Richard II at Mile End. Tyler represented the convergence of specific short-term grievances — the Poll Tax, the French Wars’ failures — with the deeper, longer-term anger about serfdom and inequality that John Ball had given intellectual expression.

The Peasants’ Revolt began in Essex and Kent for specific reasons. Both counties had experienced aggressive enforcement of the Statute of Labourers. Both had relatively prosperous peasant communities with enough resources to organise resistance. Essex was close to the legal records and institutions the rebels targeted in London; Kent was the route through which French raids had recently threatened the coast, making taxation for failed wars especially bitter. The arrival of Poll Tax commissioners in these specific counties acted as the detonator for grievances that had been accumulating for decades.

lesson_title: The Peasants' Revolt: events of May-June 1381
content_html:
The Revolt Begins: Essex and Kent, May 1381

The immediate trigger for the Peasants’ Revolt came in late May 1381, when government tax commissioners arrived in the village of Brentwood in Essex to investigate non-payment of the Poll Tax. The villagers drove the commissioner out. News of this defiance spread rapidly. Within days, communities across Essex were in open resistance, and the rebellion in Kent was igniting in parallel. Wat Tyler emerged as the leader of the Kentish rebels, marshalling thousands into a disciplined force.

The revolt was not simply a mob. The rebels marched with organisation, targeted specific institutions (the records of serfdom, the property of corrupt officials) and articulated clear political demands. Their anger was directed not at the king himself — the fourteen-year-old Richard II was initially presented as a potential ally against bad advisers — but at the system that kept them in servitude.

Key Fact

The Peasants’ Revolt began in Brentwood, Essex in late May 1381 when tax commissioners were driven out. Within days, rebels from Essex and Kent were marching on London, led respectively by figures from each county with Wat Tyler leading the Kentish contingent.

The March on London and the Tower

By early June 1381, the rebel armies had converged on London. The city’s gates were opened by sympathisers within, and the rebels entered. They targeted properties associated with their enemies: the palace of the Savoy (belonging to John of Gaunt, the king’s uncle and the most powerful noble in England) was burned to the ground. Law courts and legal records — the documents that defined serfs’ legal obligations — were destroyed. The Tower of London was breached on 13–14 June 1381. The rebels dragged out Archbishop Sudbury — who as Lord Chancellor was associated with the hated poll taxes — and executed him on Tower Hill, along with the Lord Treasurer Robert Hales.

John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, was the most powerful noble in England and effectively one of the men guiding government during the minority of Richard II. He was widely blamed for corruption and for the direction of the failing French Wars. He also represented the most extreme end of noble privilege. Burning his palace — though the rebels reportedly forbade actual looting, turning violence towards a symbolic act of destruction rather than theft — was a powerful political statement about who the rebels held responsible for their condition.

The Meeting at Mile End, 14 June 1381

On 14 June 1381, Richard II rode out to meet the rebels at Mile End. Facing thousands of angry rebels, the fourteen-year-old king showed remarkable composure. He agreed to the rebels’ principal demands: the abolition of serfdom, a fixed low rent for land, freedom to trade, and a pardon for all the rebels. Richard even had charters drawn up on the spot granting these terms.

Many Essex rebels, satisfied that their demands had been met, began to leave London. But the revolt was not yet over. The Kentish contingent under Wat Tyler remained, with additional demands. Tyler and his followers held the city, and the key confrontation was yet to come.

Key Fact

At Mile End on 14 June 1381, Richard II promised the rebels the abolition of serfdom, the freedom to trade and a pardon for all participants. He had charters drawn up immediately — but these promises were all subsequently withdrawn after the revolt was suppressed.

Smithfield and the Death of Wat Tyler, 15 June 1381

The following day, 15 June 1381, Richard II met the Kentish rebels at Smithfield. Wat Tyler rode forward alone to present the rebels’ demands, which went beyond the concessions at Mile End: the distribution of Church wealth, the abolition of all lordship except the king’s, and equality before the law. During the tense negotiations, a confrontation broke out. Tyler was struck by the Mayor of London, William Walworth, and fatally stabbed. He died at the scene.

In the moment of confusion that followed, Richard II rode forward and addressed the rebels directly: “You shall have no captain but me.” Whether through the king’s authority, the shock of Tyler’s death, or the arrival of loyalist forces from the city, the rebel army dispersed. With Tyler dead and the leadership gone, the revolt in London collapsed.

Revolt continued in Norfolk, Suffolk, Hertfordshire and other parts of England through June 1381. Henry Despenser, Bishop of Norwich, led a military force that brutally suppressed the rebellion in East Anglia. John Ball was captured, tried and executed in July 1381. Royal commissions travelled the counties, trying and executing rebel leaders — historians estimate that several hundred people were killed in the reprisals, though precise numbers are uncertain. The charters granted at Mile End were revoked. Richard II, when pressed to honour his promises, reportedly said: “Villeins you are and villeins you shall remain.” Whether he used these exact words is disputed, but the sentiment expressed the ruling class’s determination to restore the old order.

lesson_title: Significance of the Peasants' Revolt
content_html:
Was 1381 a Failure or a Beginning?

At first glance, the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 looks like a comprehensive failure. The rebels were defeated, their leader killed, their charters revoked. Hundreds were executed in the reprisals that followed. Serfdom was not abolished. The Poll Tax, though withdrawn, was replaced by other forms of taxation. Yet historians have argued that the revolt’s long-term significance was profound — that it marked a turning point in the relationship between rulers and ruled, even if the immediate results were suppression and disappointment.

Richard’s Broken Promises

Almost immediately after the revolt was crushed, Richard II withdrew every concession he had made at Mile End. The Mile End charters were cancelled. Peasants who had believed their freedom was secured returned to find nothing had changed legally. Richard’s reported words — whether or not he used exactly these — that “villeins you are and villeins you shall remain” captured the ruling class’s collective determination to restore the pre-revolt order.

Parliament also revoked any concessions made under duress, and the Poll Tax was never levied again in this form — one concrete and lasting concession. But the broader legal framework of serfdom remained intact in law, even if it was being eroded in practice.

Key Fact

The immediate aftermath: the Poll Tax was never levied again; all the Mile End charters were revoked; serfdom remained legal; hundreds of rebels were executed. The revolt achieved only one immediate concrete gain — the abandonment of the Poll Tax — but its longer-term significance was much greater.

The Decline of Serfdom

Although serfdom was not legally abolished in 1381, it continued to decline steadily over the following century. The revolt had demonstrated, dramatically, that the peasantry would resist when pushed too far. Lords who might have considered reasserting their rights by force after the revolt faced a less cooperative and more assertive peasantry. The practical economics of the post-plague labour market continued to work against serfdom: it remained more economical for most lords to convert labour obligations to money rents than to try to enforce them.

By the mid-fifteenth century, the decline of serfdom was well advanced across much of England, though it was never abolished by a single act of Parliament. Historians debate the precise role the revolt played in this process: some argue it accelerated the pace of change; others that the economic forces set in motion by the Black Death would have produced the same outcome regardless. The consensus is that 1381 was one significant factor in a long structural change.

Despite the violent suppression of 1381, the peasantry did not retreat into passivity. The revolt had demonstrated that collective action was possible — that ordinary people could march on London, force a king to negotiate and make the ruling class fear for its position. This assertiveness did not evaporate. Local resistance to labour obligations continued across England throughout the later fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The revolt’s memory became part of a broader tradition of popular protest in English history.

Control of Wages After 1381

Parliament continued to attempt to control wages after 1381, passing further legislation in line with the original Statute of Labourers. But the practical effectiveness of wage controls diminished. The labour shortage that the Black Death had created persisted well into the fifteenth century, and the economic forces pushing wages up were simply stronger than the law could overcome. By the early fifteenth century, real wages for agricultural workers were higher than they had been before the Black Death — a quiet economic victory that had been fought for in the fields, on the roads to London, and at Smithfield.

Key Fact

The revolt’s long-term significance: the Poll Tax was abandoned; serfdom declined gradually over the following century; real wages rose; and the revolt demonstrated that the peasantry would resist political exploitation — a lesson that shaped how subsequent rulers calculated what they could demand from their subjects.

Effects on the Hundred Years’ War

The revolt had direct consequences for England’s conduct of the Hundred Years’ War. The years around 1381 marked a period of significant English military setback in France, as Charles V’s campaigns had recovered much of the territory won by Edward III and the Black Prince. The fiscal crisis that had produced the Poll Tax — the need to fund a failing war — had contributed directly to revolt at home.

After 1381, the government was far more cautious about imposing heavy direct taxation, particularly on the poorest. This constrained the resources available for military campaigns in France. The revolt thus indirectly reduced the financial pressure that could be put on the poorest for war — not because the ruling class had become more sympathetic, but because they had learned that there were limits to what they could extract.

The revolt also marked a significant moment in the history of political consciousness in England. The rebels articulated specific demands — the abolition of serfdom, freedom to trade, equality before the law — in a context where ordinary people did not have formal political representation. The act of marching to London, forcing the king to negotiate and articulating a programme of reform was itself significant, regardless of the immediate outcome. Historians who see the revolt as part of a long tradition of popular politics in England often point to 1381 as a foundational moment.

lesson_title: Interpretations: was 1381 a failed revolution or a turning point?
content_html:
Why Interpretations Differ

The Peasants’ Revolt of 1381 has been interpreted in widely different ways over the past six hundred years. The question of whether 1381 was a failed revolution or a genuine turning point is not simply a matter of selecting facts — it depends on what the historian considers important, what sources they rely on, and when they are writing. Understanding why historians disagree is a core skill for this paper, because “why do interpretations differ?” questions require you to analyse the reasoning behind an argument, not just describe what it says.

Traditional and Conservative Readings

For much of the medieval period and into the early modern era, the revolt was read through the lens of its immediate failure. Chronicles written by monastic authors and members of the literate establishment described the rebels as dangerous, deluded and ultimately deserving of defeat. The conservative reading of the revolt emphasised that the existing social order was divinely ordained, that the rebels were guilty of treason, and that their punishment was just. From this viewpoint, 1381 was not a turning point but a warning of what happens when social order breaks down.

Some later historians also stressed the revolt’s limited and confused aims. They argued that the rebels had no coherent ideology — only grievances — and that their demands at Mile End were too vague and unrealistic to constitute a genuine revolutionary programme. On this reading, 1381 was important as a sign of social tension but not as a transformative event in English history.

Key Fact

The conservative reading of 1381 stresses immediate failure: the revolt was crushed, leaders executed, promises revoked. It tends to use chronicle sources written by establishment figures who were hostile to the rebels. This reading asks: what changed in law? Answer: very little. It therefore concludes 1381 was significant only as evidence of discontent, not as a turning point.

The Marxist Reading: Class War and Its Limits

From the late nineteenth century onwards, a very different reading emerged. Historians influenced by Marxist historiography saw the Peasants’ Revolt as an early and important example of class struggle — the exploited peasantry rising against a ruling class that used law, serfdom and taxation to extract their surplus labour. For these historians, the revolt was significant not because it succeeded immediately but because it demonstrated that the peasantry had developed class consciousness: a sense of collective identity and shared interest in challenging their oppressors.

Rodney Hilton, whose 1973 study “Bond Men Made Free” is the most influential Marxist analysis of the revolt, argued that 1381 was central to the long-term decline of serfdom. The revolt showed lords that the costs of enforcing serfdom by coercion were too high — a calculation that contributed to their gradual acceptance of money rents. Hilton saw the revolt as a turning point in the liberation of the English peasantry, even though it was violently suppressed.

Rodney Hilton (1916–2002) was a British medieval historian at the University of Birmingham, associated with the Marxist social history school. His interpretation of the revolt was written at a time when social history — studying the lives of ordinary people rather than kings and battles — was becoming an important methodology. Hilton’s focus on the structural economic conditions of serfdom, and on what the revolt revealed about peasant consciousness, reflected the intellectual context of the 1970s. A historian writing in a period of labour movement activism would naturally be drawn to evidence of historical working-class resistance.

The Whig Reading: Progress and Popular Politics

A third tradition, associated with the broadly Whig interpretation of English history, sees 1381 as a foundational moment in a long story of expanding popular political rights. On this reading, the revolt mattered because it demonstrated that ordinary people could force their way into the political arena — that the king could be made to negotiate, that grievances could be articulated as demands, and that collective action was possible.

This reading has been criticised for reading too much democratic intention back into the revolt — the rebels did not want parliamentary representation or universal suffrage; they wanted the abolition of serfdom and lower taxes. But the Whig tradition’s emphasis on 1381 as a moment of political consciousness has proved durable: the revolt is regularly cited in accounts of English popular politics alongside the Levellers, the Chartists and later working-class movements.

Key Fact

Interpretations of 1381 differ because historians write from different intellectual and political contexts. A Marxist historian writing in the 1970s during a period of labour movement activity reads 1381 as class struggle; a conservative historian writing in the 1880s emphasising social order reads it as dangerous riot; a social historian in the 2000s emphasising ordinary lives reads it as evidence of peasant agency and political consciousness.

Why Do Interpretations Differ? The Core Analysis

To answer a “why do interpretations differ?” question on the Peasants’ Revolt, you need to identify the specific reasons behind different historians’ conclusions. The main factors are:

Sources used: medieval chronicle sources were written by establishment figures hostile to the rebels; modern social historians use manor court records, legal documents and economic data that reveal a different picture of peasant conditions and agency.

Time of writing: a historian writing in 1400 saw a defeated revolt; a historian writing in 1973 could trace the subsequent decline of serfdom and argue Hilton’s thesis about its long-term impact.

Methodological approach: historians who focus on political events (what happened in Parliament, what laws were passed) reach different conclusions from those who focus on social and economic change (what happened to wages, rents, serf numbers over decades).

Later historians such as Christopher Dyer have sought a middle path between the “failed revolt” and “turning point” readings. Dyer’s work on the English peasantry emphasises that peasant assertiveness — in manor courts, in wage negotiations and in small-scale daily resistance — was as historically significant as the dramatic events of 1381. On this view, the revolt was one episode in a longer process of peasant agency that had been transforming English rural society since the Black Death. It was important but not uniquely transformative: the structural forces already in motion would have produced change regardless.

lesson_title: Exam technique and synthesis: sources, interpretations and judgements
content_html:
Bringing the Unit Together

This lesson synthesises the whole unit — the Hundred Years’ War, the Black Death, and the Peasants’ Revolt — and focuses on the specific exam skills you need to perform well on source and interpretation questions. These questions test different abilities from straightforward recall: they ask you to evaluate evidence, analyse reasoning and construct a substantiated judgement.

Source Utility: The Three-Element Test

A source utility question asks you how useful a source is for a specific enquiry. The most common student mistake is to judge usefulness purely on the basis of who wrote it — “the source is biased because it was written by a monk who supported the king.” This approach caps your marks. A high-mark answer uses all three elements:

Content: What does the source actually say? What specific information does it give you? Summarise and select the relevant detail for the enquiry.

Provenance: Who wrote it, when, and why? What is their likely viewpoint, and how does that affect what they chose to include or omit? A lord’s account of the revolt will emphasise different things from a rebel’s.

Own knowledge: Does what you know about the period support, challenge or add context to the source? This is where your unit knowledge becomes actively useful. If the source describes the Black Death causing labour shortages, you can confirm or nuance this with what you know about the Statute of Labourers.

Key Fact

High-mark source utility answers integrate all three elements: content (what the source says), provenance (who wrote it, when and why), and own contextual knowledge (what you know that helps you judge the source). A response that addresses only one or two of these cannot reach the top band.

Compare Interpretations: Why, Not Just What

The most common error on compare interpretations questions is explaining how two interpretations differ rather than why they differ. These are fundamentally different tasks.

Explaining how they differ: “Interpretation A says the revolt was a failure because serfdom was not abolished. Interpretation B says it was a turning point because serfdom declined over the following century.” This is description — it tells the examiner you can read, but it does not engage with the historians’ reasoning.

Explaining why they differ: “Interpretation A was written using chronicle sources hostile to the rebels, leading the author to emphasise immediate suppression. Interpretation B, written in 1973 by a social historian drawing on manor court records, could trace the long-term economic changes unavailable to chronicle writers — which is why their conclusions differ.” This is analysis: it identifies the reasons behind the difference.

Imagine a question: “How useful is Source A for an historian studying the causes of the Peasants’ Revolt?” Source A is a chronicle written by a monk at St Albans Abbey in 1382 describing rebels as “the lowest of the low, incited by the devil.”

Content: The source tells us the rebels were widely seen by the establishment as dangerous criminals motivated by evil. This is useful for understanding how the ruling class perceived the revolt.

Provenance: Written by a monk in 1382 — one year after the revolt. Monks were part of the Church establishment, which suffered during the revolt (Archbishop Sudbury was killed). This author had strong reasons to portray the rebels negatively. This limits the source’s usefulness for understanding the rebels’ own motivations.

Own knowledge: I know that the rebels had specific political demands (abolition of serfdom, the Mile End programme) and were responding to the Poll Tax and Statute of Labourers. The source’s dismissal of their motives is therefore one-sided, but its very hostility tells us something useful about the establishment’s response to popular revolt.

Evaluate an Interpretation: Agree AND Disagree

For 12-mark “evaluate an interpretation” questions, the most common error is pure agreement or pure disagreement. You must argue both ways using your own knowledge, then reach a substantiated overall judgement. The mark scheme rewards:

1. Developed points in support of the interpretation, using specific factual evidence.
2. Developed points that challenge or qualify the interpretation, using specific factual evidence.
3. A clear overall judgement that explains which view you find more convincing and why.

Example: if asked how far you agree that “the Black Death was the main cause of the Peasants’ Revolt,” you would argue in support (labour shortages → Statute of Labourers → resentment; population decline changed economic balance) and against (the Poll Tax of 1380 and the cost of the French Wars were more immediate triggers; John Ball’s ideas had a direct role), before reaching a judgement about whether long-term structural change or short-term triggers were more important.

Key Fact

A substantiated overall judgement does not simply say “I partly agree.” It explains the basis for the conclusion: “The Black Death was a necessary precondition of the revolt — without the labour shortage and resentment it created, the Poll Tax alone would not have triggered mass rebellion — but the immediate cause was the fiscal pressure of the French Wars and the injustice of the 1380 Poll Tax, making the Black Death the more fundamental long-term cause rather than the most important single factor.”

The Extended Essay: Period Essay Structure

For 16-mark period essays covering this unit, the key requirement is a substantiated judgement on the specific question asked. A common mistake is to cover two or three factors adequately but fail to weigh them against each other. The top band is reached by arguing why one factor was more significant than others — not by covering everything.

Structure: brief introduction that signals your overall argument; main paragraphs each organised around one factor or theme with embedded evidence; a conclusion that directly answers the question with a clear, justified overall judgement. The conclusion should not simply repeat your introduction — it should emerge from the argument you have just made.

Writing in the first person or as a narrative (“I was a peasant in 1381 and I felt angry”) caps your analytical marks — extended responses must be written as historical analysis, not creative writing. Covering only one side of the argument prevents you reaching the top band on “how far do you agree?” questions — you must always acknowledge and engage with the counter-argument. Beginning every paragraph with the same sentence structure (“Another reason was...”) signals a list rather than an argument — instead, each paragraph should build on the previous one and contribute to your overall case.

lesson_title: Elizabethan government: court, Privy Council and Parliament
content_html:
Elizabeth I: Coronation and Early Reign

On 17 November 1558, Elizabeth I became Queen of England at the age of twenty-five. She was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 15 January 1559. Her accession was welcomed by many English people who had grown weary of the religious upheavals and foreign entanglements of her half-sister Mary I’s reign. Elizabeth was seen as a Protestant hope, young and English-born. Her early popularity was genuine — crowds lined the streets for her coronation procession, and she responded warmly, reportedly saying that the love of her subjects was more precious than any treasure.

Key Fact

Elizabeth was crowned on 15 January 1559. Within months she passed the Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity, establishing her control over the Church of England and setting the style of worship. This swift action showed her ability to govern decisively from the start of her reign.

The Royal Court

The Royal Court was the heart of Elizabethan government. It was wherever Elizabeth happened to be — at Whitehall Palace, Hampton Court, Greenwich or on one of her summer ‘progresses’ through the country. The court served two purposes: it was both a centre of pageantry designed to project royal power, and a practical arena where political decisions were made and favour was dispensed.

Nobles competed intensely to attend the Queen because proximity to Elizabeth meant access to patronage — the granting of offices, grants of land, or licences to trade. Those who lost favour could lose everything. This system gave Elizabeth enormous political leverage: she could reward loyalty and punish disloyalty simply by controlling access to her presence. Favourites such as Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, and later Robert Devereux, Earl of Essex, gained influence through personal closeness to the Queen rather than formal office alone.

The Privy Council

The Privy Council was Elizabeth’s main governing body. It typically comprised around nineteen members — senior nobles, lawyers and churchmen — who met several times a week to advise the Queen, administer royal policy and handle correspondence. The Council had real power: it could issue proclamations, summon individuals for questioning and direct local officials.

The most influential councillor throughout much of Elizabeth’s reign was William Cecil, who served first as Secretary of State (1558–1572) and then as Lord Treasurer until his death in 1598. Cecil was cautious, Protestant and deeply loyal. He gathered intelligence through an extensive network of spies and helped Elizabeth navigate plots and crises. Elizabeth trusted him above all others, though she did not always follow his advice — particularly on the question of marriage and succession.

Sir Francis Walsingham served as Principal Secretary from 1573 until his death in 1590. A committed Puritan, he ran the government’s intelligence service and was responsible for uncovering the Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots against the Queen. Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, was Elizabeth’s favourite courtier and sat on the Council for many years; he commanded the English forces sent to the Netherlands in 1585. After Cecil’s death, his son Robert Cecil effectively took over the management of government, serving as Secretary of State from 1596 and eventually smoothing the succession of James VI of Scotland in 1603.

Local Government: Justices of the Peace

Beyond the court and Council, Elizabeth governed England through a network of Justices of the Peace. These were unpaid local gentlemen appointed by the Crown to serve in each county. By the end of the reign there were approximately 50–60 JPs in each county, and their responsibilities were vast: they enforced the law at quarter sessions, collected taxes, regulated wages, oversaw the poor relief system and ensured that royal proclamations were carried out.

The JP system was both the strength and the weakness of Elizabethan local government. It was cheap, and it bound the local gentry into the royal system — serving as a JP was a mark of social status that gentlemen competed for. However, the Crown depended on men it could not directly control. A JP who was sympathetic to Catholicism or reluctant to enforce unpopular policies could simply drag his feet. Elizabeth had no standing army or professional police force to enforce her will; she relied on willing cooperation.

Key Fact

Justices of the Peace were the backbone of Elizabethan local government — unpaid gentry who carried out royal orders in each county. Because they were unpaid and locally rooted, the Crown could not guarantee their full compliance, making local enforcement uneven.

Parliament: Role and Limitations

Parliament in Elizabethan England was very different from Parliament today. It had two chambers — the Lords (nobles and bishops) and the Commons (elected burgesses and knights of the shire) — but it was not a permanent institution. Elizabeth summoned Parliament only when she needed it, typically to grant taxation or to pass laws on matters that required its authority. During her forty-five-year reign she called Parliament only thirteen times, and for a total of fewer than four years in session.

Elizabeth was acutely aware of Parliament’s potential to challenge her authority. She refused to allow MPs to debate matters she considered her personal prerogative: religion, her marriage, and the succession. When Peter Wentworth raised the issue of free speech in Parliament in 1576, Elizabeth had him imprisoned in the Tower. She insisted that freedom of speech in Parliament meant freedom to discuss matters she had already introduced, not freedom to raise whatever MPs wished.

Parliament’s most important constitutional function was granting taxation. The Crown’s ordinary revenues — from royal estates, customs duties and feudal dues — were rarely sufficient to fund war or extraordinary expenditure. Elizabeth therefore called Parliament when she needed ‘subsidies’ voted by the Commons. Parliament used this power carefully; it could, in theory, refuse a subsidy or attach conditions. In practice, Elizabeth managed Parliament skillfully, using a network of ‘privy councillors’ who sat as MPs and managed debates. She also relied on the Speaker of the House of Commons (effectively a Crown appointee in this period) to steer business.

lesson_title: Lifestyles of rich and poor
content_html:
A Society of Stark Contrasts

Elizabethan England was a society of striking inequality. A small number of landowners — the nobility and gentry — enjoyed wealth, fine houses and elaborate fashions, while at the bottom of society a growing number of the poor struggled to survive. The gap between these extremes widened during the sixteenth century, largely because of rising population, inflation and changes in agriculture. Understanding this contrast is central to understanding the Elizabethan age.

The Lives of the Wealthy

The Elizabethan period saw a wave of great country house building. The great houses built by nobles and wealthy gentry were statements of power and loyalty. Houses such as Hardwick Hall in Derbyshire (built by Bess of Hardwick, completed 1597) and Burghley House in Lincolnshire (built by William Cecil) were designed to impress — and to accommodate the Queen on her summer progresses. Large windows — glass being expensive — were a mark of wealth, leading to the saying “Hardwick Hall, more glass than wall.”

Inside these houses, the wealthy enjoyed lavish feasting. Banquets could last for hours, featuring meat, game, spiced dishes, elaborate sugar sculptures and imported wines. The wealthiest kept their own deer parks for hunting and employed large numbers of servants. A great noble’s household might contain dozens of staff — stewards, cooks, grooms, ladies-in-waiting and more — all reflecting the master’s status.

Dress in Elizabethan England was not merely personal taste — it was a public statement of rank. Sumptuary laws regulated what each social class could wear, reserving certain colours and fabrics for the highest ranks. Purple silk and gold cloth of gold were restricted to royalty. The ruff — the distinctive pleated collar of linen or lace — became a hallmark of the Elizabethan age, growing ever larger and more elaborate across the reign. Wealthy women wore the farthingale, a hooped underskirt that gave skirts their wide, structured shape. These fashions were expensive, time-consuming to maintain and deliberately impractical — they advertised that their wearer did not need to do physical work.

The Lives of the Poor

For the majority of Elizabethans — tenant farmers, labourers, craftsmen and their families — life was far harder. Most people lived in modest timber-framed cottages, working long hours in agriculture or craft trades. Their diet was plain: bread, pottage (a thick vegetable and grain stew), cheese and occasional meat. A poor harvest could mean genuine hunger.

Below the working poor sat an even more desperate group: the vagabonds and vagrants. A rising population — from around 2.8 million in 1551 to approximately 4.1 million by 1601 — combined with inflation (prices rose sharply throughout the reign), enclosures of common land, and the dissolution of the monasteries (which had previously provided some charity) created a growing pool of the homeless and unemployed. Contemporaries feared vagrants as a threat to social order and distinguished between the “impotent poor” (those who could not work due to age, disability or sickness) and the “sturdy beggars” (those deemed capable of work but unwilling to find it).

Key Fact

Four main causes drove the rise of vagrancy: population growth, inflation (rising prices outpacing wages), enclosures of common land (removing livelihoods from rural labourers), and the dissolution of the monasteries under Henry VIII (removing a traditional source of poor relief).

Government Legislation: The Poor Laws

The Elizabethan government’s response to poverty evolved across the reign. Early measures were harsh: the 1547 Vagrancy Act under Edward VI had briefly enslaved persistent vagrants, though this was quickly repealed. Tudor attitudes were complex — the government felt genuine pity for the “impotent poor” but fear and hostility towards the able-bodied vagrant. A series of poor laws attempted to separate these groups and deal with each differently.

The culmination of Elizabethan poor law legislation came with the 1601 Poor Law (formally the Act for the Relief of the Poor). This act established a national framework by placing responsibility for poor relief on each parish. Overseers of the Poor were appointed in every parish to collect a compulsory “poor rate” from householders and distribute it as follows: the impotent poor (elderly, sick, disabled) received “outdoor relief” — money or goods to allow them to survive at home; the able-bodied poor who genuinely could not find work were to be set to work (in a “house of correction”); and the “idle poor” (sturdy beggars who refused work) were to be punished.

Key Fact

The 1601 Poor Law was landmark legislation: it created a compulsory poor rate in every parish, appointed Overseers of the Poor, and distinguished between the impotent poor (to be helped), the able-bodied unemployed (to be set to work) and idle vagrants (to be punished). It remained the basis of English poor relief for over two hundred years.

The 1601 Poor Law was genuinely significant in the long term. It was the first national, compulsory system of poor relief in English history — a shift from voluntary charity to state obligation. It remained largely in force until the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834. However, its significance in the short term should not be overstated: implementation was uneven, depending on the willingness of local parish officers, and the law did little to address the root causes of poverty such as enclosure and inflation. Critics argue it was more concerned with controlling the poor than genuinely relieving suffering.

lesson_title: Popular entertainment in Elizabethan times
content_html:
Entertainment in Elizabethan England

Entertainment in Elizabethan England reflected the sharp divisions of society. The wealthy enjoyed elaborate banquets, hunting, jousting and masques at court, while ordinary people found pleasure in sports, festivals, taverns and, increasingly, the professional theatre. Both groups shared a taste for some forms of entertainment that modern audiences find uncomfortable — particularly the cruel animal sports that drew large crowds across the country.

Cruel Sports: Bear-Baiting and Cock-Fighting

Bear-baiting was one of the most popular entertainments of the age, enjoyed by people of all social classes — including Elizabeth I herself. A bear would be chained to a post in a circular arena (a “bear garden”) and set upon by trained dogs. London had several bear gardens on the south bank of the Thames, near what would become the theatre district. Cock-fighting was equally widespread, with purpose-built cockpits in many towns. Both sports involved gambling, which added to their appeal for spectators at all social levels.

These entertainments were not considered cruel in the way we would regard them today. They were a normal part of Elizabethan life, enjoyed on public holidays and Sundays. Puritans objected, but largely on moral grounds: they worried that such entertainments drew people away from church attendance and encouraged idleness and gambling, rather than expressing concern for the animals.

Key Fact

Bear-baiting was enjoyed by all social classes, including Elizabeth I. Puritans opposed it not for reasons of animal welfare but because it encouraged idleness and gambling, and drew people away from church on Sundays.

Entertainment for the Wealthy

The Elizabethan nobility and upper gentry enjoyed a range of pastimes unavailable to ordinary people. Hunting and hawking required land, horses and trained birds — luxuries of the rich. The royal court was a centre of culture: music, dancing and poetry were all prized accomplishments. Elizabeth I herself was an accomplished musician and dancer. Court masques were lavish productions combining music, dance, poetry and magnificent costumes. Tournaments and jousting continued into the early years of Elizabeth’s reign, though they declined in popularity as the century progressed. For those below the highest nobility, bowling, tennis and archery were popular, with archery practice actually required by law for men of certain ages.

The Rise of the Elizabethan Theatre

The most significant cultural development of the Elizabethan age was the rise of the professional playhouse. Before this period, plays were performed by travelling companies in inn yards, market squares or at court. The first permanent public playhouse in England, known simply as “The Theatre,” was built in Shoreditch, London, in 1576 by James Burbage. This was a pivotal moment: it created a permanent commercial theatre industry. More playhouses followed — the Curtain (1577), the Rose (1587), the Swan (c.1595) and, most famously, the Globe Theatre, built in Southwark in 1599 by the company known as the Lord Chamberlain’s Men.

Elizabethan playhouses were typically circular or polygonal wooden structures with a central open-air yard. The stage projected into this yard, and three tiers of covered galleries surrounded it. ‘Groundlings’ — ordinary people who paid a penny — stood in the open yard around the stage, while wealthier patrons sat in the covered galleries. The stage was large and thrust into the audience, allowing for different acting areas and creating intimacy. There was no scenery in the modern sense; location was established through words and the audience’s imagination. Performances took place in the afternoon by natural light. Audiences were mixed and lively — eating, drinking, talking and reacting noisily.

Key Fact

The first permanent public playhouse in England was “The Theatre,” built in Shoreditch, London, in 1576 by James Burbage. The Globe Theatre, built in Southwark in 1599, became the most famous Elizabethan playhouse and was closely associated with William Shakespeare.

Attitudes Towards the Theatre

Not everyone welcomed the new playhouses. The Puritans strongly opposed the theatre on moral and religious grounds. They argued that plays encouraged immorality, that theatres were dens of crime and disease, and that performances on Sundays competed with church attendance. London’s city authorities largely agreed, which is why the early playhouses were built just outside the city boundaries — in the “Liberties,” areas beyond the jurisdiction of the city council.

In 1597 the city authorities briefly ordered the demolition of all London’s playhouses, though this was never fully carried out. The theatre had powerful patrons, however: noble families sponsored acting companies (the Chamberlain’s Men were under the patronage of the Lord Chamberlain, and later became the King’s Men under James I). Elizabeth herself enjoyed theatrical performances; she had plays performed at court regularly. This royal favour helped protect the theatre industry from its opponents.

William Shakespeare (1564–1616) was the most celebrated playwright of the Elizabethan age, though he was one of many talented writers working in this period. Christopher Marlowe, Ben Jonson and Thomas Kyd were among his contemporaries. Plays ranged from histories (presenting English kings and their struggles) to tragedies, comedies and romances. The popular appeal of theatre was broad: a wealthy patron and a penny-paying groundling might watch the same play. This cultural breadth made the theatre unusual — few other forms of entertainment crossed so many social boundaries.

lesson_title: The Religious Settlement of 1559
content_html:
The Religious Problem in 1558

When Elizabeth came to the throne in November 1558, England was a country torn by religious conflict. Henry VIII had broken with Rome in the 1530s and made himself Supreme Head of the Church of England; Edward VI’s reign had pushed England towards a more clearly Protestant settlement; and Mary I had returned England to papal obedience and burned nearly 300 Protestants. By 1558 the country had been through four different religious settlements in twenty-five years. Elizabeth needed to act swiftly and carefully to restore stability.

The religious landscape Elizabeth inherited was deeply divided. Committed Protestants (many returning from exile in Protestant Europe) wanted a thorough reformation. Many ordinary English people — especially in the north and west — remained attached to traditional Catholic practice. A significant number of Catholic clergy refused to swear loyalty to a Protestant queen. The Pope, and England’s main Catholic neighbours France and Spain, watched closely. Any settlement Elizabeth chose would alienate someone.

Elizabeth’s Aims: The ‘Middle Way’

Elizabeth’s approach to religion has been described as the Middle Way — a settlement designed to be broadly inclusive. She wanted a Church that was Protestant in its key doctrines (rejecting papal authority and the Catholic doctrine of transubstantiation) but that retained enough traditional ceremony to be acceptable to moderate Catholics. Her aim was political stability rather than theological purity. Elizabeth appears to have had genuine personal religious views, but she was above all a pragmatist who wanted a peaceful kingdom.

Key Fact

Elizabeth’s religious aims were: to establish her own authority over the Church of England (replacing the Pope), and to set a uniform style of worship that most English people could accept. These aims were delivered by the Act of Supremacy and the Act of Uniformity, both passed in 1559.

The Act of Supremacy, 1559

The Act of Supremacy was passed by Parliament in April 1559. It formally re-established the English Church’s independence from Rome and gave Elizabeth the title ‘Supreme Governor’ of the Church of England. Note the subtle but important distinction: Henry VIII had been ‘Supreme Head’, but Elizabeth chose ‘Supreme Governor’ — a less sweeping claim that was more acceptable to those who doubted a woman could be the spiritual head of the Church.

All clergy and royal officials were required to swear an oath recognising Elizabeth’s supremacy. Those who refused could be fined or imprisoned. Most of the Marian clergy eventually conformed, though several bishops who had served under Mary refused and were deprived of their positions. The Act effectively dismantled papal authority in England for the second time.

The Act of Uniformity, 1559

The Act of Uniformity was passed in the same month. It made attendance at Church of England services compulsory for all English people — those who absented themselves could be fined twelve pence (a significant sum for a labourer) per absence. It also introduced a revised Book of Common Prayer, based on Thomas Cranmer’s 1552 Protestant version but with key modifications designed to be more acceptable to traditional Catholics.
