To assess a source’s utility, a historian considers three things together: content (what does it actually show or say?), provenance (who produced it, when, why, and for what audience?) and contextual knowledge (what do we already know that helps us read its significance and limits?). A recruitment poster is highly useful as evidence of government propaganda methods — but tells us little about whether those appeals worked or what soldiers genuinely believed. It must be used alongside other evidence.

Wilfred Owen wrote most of his major poems between August 1917 and September 1918 at Craiglockhart hospital in Edinburgh, where he met Siegfried Sassoon. His poem Dulce et Decorum Est describes a gas attack in graphic detail and ends by challenging the “old lie” that it is sweet and proper to die for one’s country. Owen was killed on 4 November 1918 — one week before the armistice — aged 25.

As a primary source, Owen’s poetry is valuable for understanding the psychological impact of the Western Front on educated officers. However, it is limited as evidence of typical soldiers’ attitudes: Owen was an officer, a poet, and wrote at a specific moment of disillusionment. Millions of ordinary soldiers left no comparable record. Historians of the “revisionist” school argue that focusing on the war poets creates a distorted picture that exaggerates disillusionment across the army.

Interpretations of the First World War

Historians have disagreed profoundly about the First World War. The dominant view in the 1920s and 1930s — shaped by the anti-war literature of Sassoon, Owen, and Robert Graves — presented the war as needless slaughter managed by incompetent generals who sent men to their deaths from comfortable chateaux far from the front. This “lions led by donkeys” interpretation became embedded in popular culture through plays such as Oh, What a Lovely War! (1963).

From the 1960s onwards, professional historians began to challenge this picture. John Keegan pioneered “history from below,” focusing on the experience of ordinary soldiers rather than commanders’ strategies. His The Face of Battle (1976) examined what it was actually like to be at Agincourt, Waterloo or the Somme.

Niall Ferguson, in The Pity of War (1998), made several provocative arguments: that Britain’s entry into the war was not inevitable or necessary; that the German advance could have been allowed to proceed without Britain’s involvement; and that the human cost of the war was ultimately Britain’s own choice. Ferguson’s thesis was controversial because it reversed the standard account of German aggression as the war’s primary cause. Critics argued he underestimated the genuine threat German hegemony in Europe would have posed to British interests and democracy.

The interpretations differ for several reasons: Ferguson wrote in the post-Cold War 1990s when empire and military sacrifice were less unquestionable values; he had access to archival sources unavailable to earlier historians; and he was asking a counterfactual question (“what if Britain had stayed out?”) that conventional diplomatic historians had not prioritised. This illustrates the key principle: interpretations change because historians ask different questions and write from different contexts.

Feminist Historiography of the Suffrage Campaign

The history of women’s suffrage has also been interpreted in conflicting ways. For much of the twentieth century, the Suffragettes — the WSPU and the Pankhursts — dominated the popular narrative, celebrated as heroic militants. From the 1970s onwards, feminist historians began to recover the history of the constitutional Suffragists (NUWSS), arguing that Millicent Fawcett’s patient, legal campaigning was equally or more important to eventual success.

A further debate concerns why women won the vote in 1918: was it because of militant suffragette pressure, wartime service, or a combination of long-term constitutional pressure and changed political circumstances? The answer depends partly on how much weight historians give to short-term versus long-term causes — a classic second-order concept debate that mirrors the wider question of how historians explain change.

Key Fact

Interpretations differ because historians write at different times, ask different questions, use different sources, and are influenced by the values of their era. For the 1890–1918 period, the key debates are: was the First World War necessary? Were the generals competent? Did militancy or constitutional pressure win women the vote?

lesson_title: Britain in 1918: a country transformed
content_html:
Britain in 1890 and Britain in 1918: How Much Had Changed?

In 1890 Britain stood at the height of its global power. It commanded the world’s largest empire, covering roughly one-quarter of the earth’s land surface. The House of Lords could veto any legislation. Women had no vote in parliamentary elections. The elderly poor faced the workhouse. Most workers had no protection against unemployment or sickness. By November 1918, when the armistice was signed, every one of those conditions had either changed or was in the process of changing. Assessing how and why Britain was transformed requires pulling together all the threads of the period: empire, political reform, social legislation, women’s rights, and the impact of a total war.

Key Fact

By 1918: women over 30 could vote; the House of Lords had lost its absolute veto; old age pensions and national insurance existed; Britain had fought the most costly war in its history; and the Boer War had exposed cracks in imperial confidence. The transformation was real but uneven — many inequalities remained.

Empire Questioned

The Second Boer War (1899–1902) marked the beginning of a change in British attitudes to empire. The concentration camps, the humiliating early defeats, and the cost in lives and money had exposed the gap between imperial rhetoric and reality. By 1902 a significant “pro-Boer” movement had shown that imperial wars were no longer automatically popular. Yet the empire did not collapse in this period — it actually grew as Germany lost its colonies in 1918. The shift was more subtle: from unquestioned confidence to contested necessity.

The First World War reinforced this ambiguity. Soldiers from India, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Africa fought and died for an empire in which they had limited political rights. The Indian and Dominion contributions — including the battles of Gallipoli (Australian and New Zealand forces) and the campaigns on the Western Front — created expectations of greater autonomy that would feed directly into post-war nationalist movements. The Dominion nationalism that grew from wartime service began the long process of imperial dissolution that accelerated after 1945.

Welfare State Foundations

The Liberal reforms of 1906–1911 had established a principle that was genuinely new: the state had a duty to protect citizens from poverty caused by forces beyond their personal control. The welfare state in its full form did not arrive until after 1945, but its intellectual and legislative foundations were created in this period. Old age pensions (1908), national insurance for sickness (1911) and unemployment insurance (1911) were the key building blocks. The Booth and Rowntree surveys had provided the evidence; Lloyd George and Churchill had provided the political will.

The Parliament Act 1911 was arguably the most significant constitutional change in Britain between 1832 and 1918. It confirmed that the elected Commons, not the hereditary Lords, was the supreme legislative body. The ability to pass controversial legislation — Home Rule, welfare reform, later Welsh Church Disestablishment — without a permanent Lords veto transformed what a democratic majority could achieve. By 1918 Britain’s political system had become significantly more democratic, even if full democracy (women voting on equal terms, a fully elected second chamber) was still decades away.

Women’s Rights: A Partial but Real Advance

The Representation of the People Act 1918 was a partial victory. The age of 30 and the property requirement excluded most young working-class women — precisely those who had contributed most to the war effort in munitions factories. Full equal suffrage came only in 1928. Nevertheless, the principle that women could vote in parliamentary elections — once considered unthinkable by the majority — had been accepted. Women also entered the paid workforce in much larger numbers, had proved their capacity in professional roles, and had begun to break into higher education and professions. The change in social expectations was permanent even if legal equality lagged.

By 1918 the Labour Party had been transformed. From 29 MPs in 1906 it had grown in credibility and organisation. The war accelerated this: the Liberal Party, which had held the centre-left ground in 1914, was destroyed by the Lloyd George vs Asquith split of 1916. Labour’s willingness to participate in the wartime coalition government, followed by its adoption of a socialist constitution in 1918 (Clause IV, committing to public ownership), positioned it to become the main progressive force in British politics. The 1918 general election saw Labour win 57 seats — and within six years it would form its first government.

Continuities: What Had Not Changed

It is equally important to recognise the limits of transformation. In 1918 the majority of women still could not vote. The House of Lords still existed and still had a delaying veto. Class inequality remained stark: officers and ordinary soldiers had very different experiences of the war, and the class system had not been fundamentally altered by the Liberal reforms. The empire was still large and largely unquestioned by mainstream opinion. Poverty had been reduced at its sharpest edges by the Liberal reforms but had not been eliminated. The “transformation” of Britain by 1918 was real but selective: significant in politics and welfare, partial in gender rights, and complicated in its effect on empire.

Key Fact

A strong answer on transformation acknowledges both change and continuity. Britain in 1918 was more democratic, had a welfare safety net, and had partially extended women’s rights — but remained an imperial power with an unequal class system and far from full democracy.

lesson_title: Exam technique: handling sources from 1890-1918
content_html:
What the Exam Tests: The Key Question Types

Exam questions on this unit test a set of specific historical skills. Understanding exactly what each question type is asking — and what the most common mistakes are — is as important as knowing the content. This lesson works through the main question types, using worked examples from the period 1890–1918.

Key Fact

For Source Utility questions (5 marks), the three elements that must work together are: Content (what the source actually says), Provenance (who produced it, when, why, for what audience) and Contextual knowledge (what you know from your own learning that helps you assess the source).

Source Utility: The 5-Mark Question

The most common mistake on source utility questions is judging a source purely on bias: “This source is biased because it was written by a government minister, so it is not useful.” This always misses the point. A source’s utility must be assessed for a specific enquiry. A government propaganda poster is extremely useful as evidence of what the government wanted people to believe — its “bias” is precisely what makes it valuable for that enquiry.

A strong utility answer does three things in sequence. First, it identifies what the source says (content). Second, it comments on who produced it and why (provenance). Third, it uses own knowledge to explain what this tells us about the source’s value for the specific question asked. All three elements should be present in a single integrated judgement, not three separate bullet points.

Question: How useful is a Charles Booth survey extract (describing families in East London living on less than 21 shillings per week) for understanding the case for Liberal social reform?

Weak answer: “This source is useful because Booth was a reliable researcher. He found lots of poverty.” (No provenance, no contextual knowledge, no specific claim about utility.)

Strong answer structure: “This source is useful for understanding the case for reform because it shows [content: specific detail from extract]. Booth was a wealthy Liverpool businessman who surveyed London from the 1880s to 1903 with no financial interest in exaggerating poverty — this increases the reliability of the content [provenance]. My own knowledge confirms that Booth found roughly 30 per cent of Londoners in poverty and identified structural causes rather than personal failings, which directly influenced Liberal reform arguments after 1906 [contextual knowledge]. However, the source is limited for understanding what form the reforms should take, since Booth described the problem rather than prescribing solutions.”

The Compare Interpretations Question (10 marks)

The critical rule for this question: you must explain why the interpretations differ, not just how they differ. Describing “Interpretation A says X while Interpretation B says Y” answers the wrong question and caps your mark at the middle band.

Reasons why interpretations differ include: the time at which the historian wrote (a 1920s historian writing in the shadow of the anti-war poets will reach different conclusions from a 1990s revisionist with access to new archives); the historian’s purpose (academic history vs popular history vs political history); the evidence they prioritised (war poets vs soldiers’ diaries vs military statistics); and any political or ideological perspective that shapes their questions.

Question: Compare Interpretations A (traditional view that the First World War was necessary to resist German militarism) and B (Ferguson’s revisionist argument that Britain need not have entered) in terms of why they differ.

Weak: “Interpretation A says the war was necessary and B says it wasn’t. They differ because one agrees with the war and one doesn’t.”

Strong structure: “The interpretations differ partly because of when they were written: the traditional view was formed in a period when resisting German militarism seemed self-evidently justified; Ferguson wrote in the 1990s post-Cold War era when empire and military intervention were being reassessed across Western culture. They also differ in the questions asked: the traditional view asks ‘Was entering the war the right thing to do?’, while Ferguson asks the counterfactual ‘Was it necessary?’ — a different question that opens different evidence. Finally, they differ in the evidence used: Ferguson had access to post-war German archives showing the limits of German war aims; earlier historians did not.”

The 12-Mark and 16-Mark Essays

Both extended essays share the same requirement: a substantiated overall judgement. This means your conclusion must do more than summarise your paragraphs. It must directly answer the question with a precise claim: “The transformation of Britain was more significant in its political and welfare dimensions than in gender or imperial terms.”

Common mistakes in the 12-mark “Evaluate an Interpretation” question: writing only agreement, or only disagreement. The mark scheme explicitly requires you to “agree and disagree” with the interpretation using your own contextual knowledge. Examiners call a response that only agrees a “one-sided essay” — it cannot reach the top band regardless of how accurate the agreement is.

Key Fact

Top-band essays on transformation argue that change was significant but uneven — real in politics and welfare, partial in gender rights, and complicated in empire. A weak conclusion says “both sides have valid points.” A strong conclusion says which side is more convincing and why.

Exam Technique Checklist

Before you write your answer, check:

  • Source utility: Have I addressed content, provenance AND contextual knowledge together — not in three separate bullets?
  • Compare interpretations: Am I explaining why they differ (time, purpose, evidence, perspective) — not just what they say?
  • 12-mark evaluate: Have I agreed AND disagreed, both with specific evidence?
  • 16-mark essay: Have I reached a substantiated overall judgement that directly answers the question — not just summarised my paragraphs?
